privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: Last updated: July 2026. This policy describes how {company} collects, uses, and protects your personal information.
privacy.s1Intro: We collect information you provide directly when you register, verify your identity, or contact us:
privacy.s1Item1: Account data: name, email, country, and a generated trading account number.
privacy.s1Item2: Identity verification (KYC): government-issued ID and proof of address, as required by regulation.
privacy.s1Item3: Transaction data: deposits, withdrawals, and full trading history.
privacy.s1Item4: Technical data: IP address, device type, and usage logs, used for security and fraud prevention.
privacy.s2Item1: To open, operate, and secure your trading account.
privacy.s2Item2: To comply with AML/KYC and other legal obligations.
privacy.s2Item3: To process deposits, withdrawals, and execute your orders.
privacy.s2Item4: To provide support and improve our services.
privacy.s3Body: We do not sell your personal data. We share it only with: regulated payment processors to move your funds; identity-verification providers to complete KYC; and competent authorities where legally required to do so. All third parties are bound by confidentiality obligations.
privacy.s4Body: Personal data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Wallets are segregated from company funds. Access to personal data is restricted to authorised personnel on a least-privilege basis and is logged.
privacy.s5Body: We retain your data for as long as your account is active, and for the period required by applicable law after closure (typically 5–7 years for transaction and KYC records).
privacy.s6Body: Subject to applicable law, you may request access to, correction of, or deletion of your personal data, and you may object to or restrict certain processing. To exercise these rights, contact {email}.
privacy.s7Body: We may update this policy from time to time. Material changes will be notified by email or in-platform notice. Continued use after a change constitutes acceptance.

aml.title: Anti-Money Laundering Policy
aml.description: Last updated: July 2026. {company} is committed to preventing money laundering, terrorist financing, and financial crime.
aml.s1Body: This Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Terrorist Financing (CTF) policy sets out the procedures we follow to detect, prevent, and report attempts to use our platform for illicit purposes, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.
aml.s2Body: We perform identity verification on every customer before enabling withdrawals and full account functionality. This includes verifying a government-issued identity document and, where required, proof of address and source of funds.
aml.s3Body: For customers classified as higher risk — including those from higher-risk jurisdictions, politically exposed persons (PEPs), or those with complex ownership structures — we apply enhanced due diligence, including additional documentation and senior-management approval.
aml.s4Body: We monitor transactions for unusual or suspicious patterns, including structuring, rapid round-tripping of funds, and activity inconsistent with a customer's profile. Suspicious activity is investigated and, where required, reported to the relevant Financial Intelligence Unit.
aml.s5Body: All customers and transactions are screened against applicable sanctions lists. We do not provide services to citizens or residents of the United States, Syria, Sudan, Iran, or North Korea, or to any sanctioned individual or entity.
aml.s6Body: We retain CDD records, transaction records, and AML investigation files for a minimum of five years after the end of the customer relationship, or longer where required by law.
aml.s7Body: Suspicious transactions are reported to the competent authority. It is an offence to tip off a customer about a suspicious-activity report. Our designated AML officer oversees this policy and all reporting.
aml.s8Body: For AML enquiries, contact our compliance team at {email}.

kyc.title: Know Your Customer (KYC) Policy
kyc.description: Last updated: July 2026. To comply with regulation and protect our clients, we verify the identity of every customer.
kyc.s1Body: Identity verification protects you and the integrity of the platform. It prevents fraud, identity theft, underage trading, and the use of the platform for money laundering. Verification is a regulatory requirement, not an optional step.
kyc.s2Item1: Identity document: a valid passport, national ID card, or driving licence. The document must be legible, unexpired, and show your photo and date of birth.
kyc.s2Item2: Proof of address: a recent (under 3 months) utility bill, bank statement, or government letter showing your name and residential address.
kyc.s2Item3: Selfie: in some cases we may ask for a selfie with your document to confirm you are the holder.
kyc.s3Item1: Submit your documents via the Verification tab in your account.
kyc.s3Item2: Our compliance team reviews your submission, typically within 1–2 business days.
kyc.s3Item3: You'll be notified by email when verification is complete, approved, or if we need more information.
kyc.s4Body: Until verification is complete, your account can trade on the demo balance but withdrawals are disabled. Once verified, you unlock withdrawals, higher limits, and full account features.
kyc.s5Body: We may periodically re-verify your identity if your documents expire, your circumstances change materially, or we identify activity that warrants it. We'll notify you in advance where possible.
kyc.s6Body: Your KYC documents are encrypted at rest, access-restricted, and used solely for verification and regulatory compliance. They are never sold or shared except with verification providers and competent authorities as required by law. See our Privacy Policy for details.
kyc.s7Body: For verification queries, contact {email} or use the Verification tab in your account.

beginners.title: Beginners Guide to Trading
beginners.description: New to the markets? Start here. Everything from your first candlestick to your first managed trade — in plain language.
beginners.s1P1: The foreign exchange (forex) market is where currencies are traded. When you trade EURUSD, you're simultaneously buying euros and selling US dollars. The goal is simple: you believe the euro will rise in value against the dollar, and if it does, you profit. If it falls, you lose.
beginners.s1P2: Unlike stocks, forex has no central exchange. It trades 24 hours a day, five days a week, across global financial centres. That round-the-clock action is both its appeal and its danger — there's always a market, which means there's always risk.
beginners.s2Item1: Pip — the smallest price move a pair makes, usually the 4th decimal (0.0001). If EURUSD moves from 1.0820 to 1.0821, that's one pip.
beginners.s2Item2: Lot — your trade size. One standard lot = 100,000 units. Most beginners start with 0.01–0.10 lots.
beginners.s2Item3: Leverage — borrowed money that lets you control a large position with a small deposit. It magnifies both gains and losses, so treat it with respect.
beginners.s3Title: 3. How to read a price chart
beginners.s3P1: A candlestick chart shows four prices for each time period: the open, high, low, and close. A green (or white) candle means price closed higher than it opened — buyers won that period. A red candle means it closed lower — sellers won. The "wicks" (thin lines) show how far price pushed beyond the open and close before settling.
beginners.s3P2: Start with one timeframe — the 1-hour or 4-hour chart is ideal for beginners. Don't overcomplicate with a dozen indicators; a clean chart with price and a single moving average is plenty to begin.
beginners.s4P1: On our platform: pick a symbol from the left sidebar, set your volume (start small — 0.01 lots), then click Buy if you think the price will rise or Sell if you think it will fall. That's it. Your position appears in the bottom table, where you can watch its profit/loss in real time and close it whenever you like.
beginners.s5P1: This is the single most important lesson in trading, and most beginners ignore it until it's too late. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on a single trade. With a $10,000 account, that's at most $100–200 of risk per trade. Use a stop-loss on every position, and size your trade so that hitting your stop costs no more than your risk budget.
beginners.s5P2: The traders who survive and thrive aren't the ones who never lose — they're the ones whose losses are small and controlled. Protect your capital first; the profits will follow.
beginners.s6Item1: Open a free account — fund your account with money.
beginners.s6Item2: Place a few small trades to get comfortable with the platform.

advanced.title: Advanced Trading Guide
advanced.description: For traders who've mastered the basics. Strategy, multi-timeframe analysis, position sizing, and the psychology of consistency.
advanced.s1P1: No single timeframe tells the whole story. Professional traders analyse the same instrument on at least two timeframes: a higher timeframe (daily or H4) to define the dominant trend and key levels, and a lower timeframe (H1 or M15) to time entries with precision.
advanced.s1P2: The rule: trade in the direction of the higher timeframe trend, using the lower timeframe to find a good entry near a higher-timeframe support or resistance. This aligns your individual trades with the larger market structure — dramatically improving win rates.
advanced.s2P1: How much should you risk per trade? The naive answer ("1–2%") is a starting point, but advanced traders size positions based on edge and odds. The Kelly formula gives the theoretically optimal fraction:
advanced.s2P2: Where p is your win probability, q = 1 − p, and b is your win/loss ratio (average win ÷ average loss). In practice, traders use a fractional Kelly (¼ or ½ Kelly) — full Kelly is too volatile for real accounts. The lesson: your position size should reflect the quality of the setup, not be fixed.
advanced.s3P1: Two long positions in EURUSD and GBPUSD are not two independent trades — the pairs are highly correlated, so you're effectively doubling up on the same "dollar weakness" bet. Real risk management accounts for correlation: a portfolio of correlated positions has far higher risk than the sum of its parts suggests. Diversify across uncorrelated instruments (a currency pair, a commodity, an index) to smooth your equity curve.
advanced.s4Intro: Every trade should answer these questions in advance:
advanced.s4Item1: What is my thesis (in one sentence)?
advanced.s4Item2: At what price do I enter, and why there specifically?
advanced.s4Item3: Where is my stop-loss (where am I wrong)?
advanced.s4Item4: Where is my take-profit (what's my target)?
advanced.s4Item5: What is my risk in dollars, and is it under my 1–2% limit?
advanced.s4Item6: What would invalidate this trade before my stop is hit?
advanced.s4P2: If you can't answer all six, you don't have a trade — you have a gamble. Write it down before you click. A journal of your trades and the reasoning behind them is the single fastest way to improve.
advanced.s5P1: The hardest opponent in trading is yourself. After a losing streak, the urge to "win it back" with bigger sizes destroys more accounts than any bad strategy. After a winning streak, overconfidence does the same. The professionals don't feel less emotion — they've built systems and rules that act regardless of how they feel.
advanced.s5P2: Three habits that separate pros from the rest: (1) a written, pre-defined trading plan you follow mechanically; (2) a hard daily loss limit after which you stop trading; (3) a journal you review weekly to find your leaks. Consistency, not brilliance, is what compounds.

calculators.title: Trading Calculators
calculators.description: Plan your trades precisely. Calculate pip value, margin requirements, and potential profit before you risk a cent.
calculators.howPip: Pip value is the monetary worth of a one-pip move for your position size. It's calculated as: pip value per lot × volume (lots). For EURUSD at 0.10 lots, one pip = $1.00.
calculators.howMargin: Margin is the collateral required to open a position. With 1:100 leverage, one standard lot (100,000 units) of EURUSD requires roughly $1,000 in margin.
calculators.howProfit: Profit / Loss is the difference between your entry and exit, expressed in pips, then converted to account currency using the pip value.

fundamental.title: Fundamental Analysis
fundamental.description: Understand the 'why' behind price moves. Macro drivers, central bank policy, and economic data — interpreted for traders.
fundamental.s1Title: Interest rates: the engine of currency markets
fundamental.s1P1: Currencies are, at their core, a reflection of relative interest rates. Capital flows toward higher-yielding currencies, so a central bank that raises rates tends to strengthen its currency — and one that cuts tends to weaken it. When you trade a pair like EURUSD, you're effectively betting on the path of ECB rates versus Fed rates.
fundamental.s1P2: That's why every central bank decision and every inflation print matters. Markets don't just react to the number — they react to whether the number changes the expected path of rates. A "hawkish surprise" (rates higher than expected, or signals of fewer future cuts) is bullish for that currency; a "dovish surprise" is bearish.
fundamental.s2Title: The big three data points to watch
fundamental.card1D: The single most-watched figure. Hot inflation forces central banks to keep rates high; cooling inflation paves the way for cuts.
fundamental.card2D: A strong labour market gives a central bank room to hold rates; rising unemployment pressures them to cut.
fundamental.card3D: Robust growth supports a strong currency; recession fears drive rate-cut expectations and weakness.
fundamental.s3Title: How to trade the news (without getting caught out)
fundamental.s3Intro: The biggest moves — and the biggest traps — happen around data releases. Three rules to keep you safe:
fundamental.s3L1: Know the calendar. Never hold a large position into a high-impact release you didn't plan for. Check our Economic Calendar daily.
fundamental.s3L2: Trade the surprise, not the number. A strong jobs number that was expected barely moves the market. It's the deviation from the forecast that matters.
fundamental.s3L3: Respect the spread. Spreads widen dramatically around releases. Use limit orders, not market orders, if you must trade the print.
fundamental.s4Body: Beyond the data, currencies respond to risk sentiment. In "risk-off" moments — wars, banking stress, pandemic fears — capital flows into safe havens like the US dollar, Japanese yen, and Swiss franc, and out of growth-linked currencies like the Australian and Canadian dollars. Learning to read this risk pulse is a powerful complement to the data-driven approach above.

trend.title: Determining Trend Potential
trend.description: Gauge whether a trend has the fuel to continue — or is running on fumes. A framework combining momentum, structure, and volume.
trend.s1Title: Step 1 — Define the trend with price structure
trend.s1Body: Before you ask whether a trend will continue, confirm it exists. An uptrend is a sequence of higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend is the reverse. The moment this structure breaks — a lower low in an uptrend — the trend is in question. Draw your swing highs and lows on a chart; this simple structure does more than any single indicator.
trend.s2Intro: Momentum tells you how much conviction backs the move. The tools:
trend.s2L1: RSI (Relative Strength Index): A reading above 55 with rising peaks confirms strong bullish momentum; divergence (price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high) warns of exhaustion.
trend.s2L2: MACD: When the histogram expands in the trend's direction, momentum is building. When it contracts, the trend is losing steam.
trend.s2L3: ADX (Average Directional Index): Above 25 indicates a trending market worth trading; below 20 suggests a choppy, range-bound market to avoid or trade with mean-reversion tactics.
trend.s3Body: A trend with rising volume is a trend with institutional participation. Look for volume to expand on impulsive moves in the trend direction and contract on the counter-trend pullbacks. If price pushes to new highs on falling volume, buyers are exhausted — a classic warning sign.
trend.s4Heading: A trend has strong continuation potential when:
trend.s4L1: Price structure (HH/HL or LH/LL) is intact
trend.s4L2: Price is above (long) or below (short) a rising/falling moving average
trend.s4L3: Momentum indicators confirm with no divergence
trend.s4L4: Volume expands on impulse moves, contracts on pullbacks
trend.s4L5: No major high-impact news imminent (check the calendar)
trend.s5Body: Even the strongest trend ends. Your exit signal is the first break of structure in the opposite direction — the first lower low after a string of higher lows. Many traders give back gains by hoping for "just a bit more." Let the structure, not your emotions, tell you when the trend has changed.
